pH, KH và GH liên quan như thế nào?

facts.fact: GH (general hardness) measures the calcium and magnesium ions dissolved in the water, i.e. how hard or soft it is.
GH is the sum of dissolved alkaline earth metal ions, mainly calcium and magnesium, with traces of strontium and others; these 'hardness builders' can leave lime deposits on aquarium glass.
1 dGH equals 17.9 ppm (mg/L) of calcium carbonate equivalent.
1 °dH corresponds to 7.144 mg/l calcium or 4.346 mg/l magnesium.
Hardness classes: soft below 8.4 °dH, medium-hard 8.4 to 14 °dH, hard from 14 °dH (German detergents law classification).
Hardness scale for shrimp keepers: soft under 6 dGH, moderate 6 to 12 dGH, very hard above 12 dGH.
GH supplies minerals for fish bone development, shrimp molting, snail shells and plant growth.
Calcium and magnesium are macronutrients for plants, and calcium builds the outer skeletons of snails, crabs and shrimp.
The bacteria that break down pollutants need a certain mineral content, and so some GH.
Too many dissolved ions raise osmotic pressure on tank inhabitants, causing stress and metabolic disorders; water too poor in minerals causes deficiencies and growth problems.
Adult fish cope well with wide GH swings; 1 dGH (20 ppm) to 17 dGH (300 ppm) is fine for all adult fish.
Eggs, larvae and fry are more sensitive to GH than adults, but researchers' acceptable range is still broad, typically 20-300 ppm GH.
Fry need calcium from the water or their food for bone growth; fry on a calcium-poor diet can die in very soft water.
Poecilia velifera showed no difference in growth or mortality between 250 ppm and 18 ppm GH water.
GH of 50 mg/L or more usually goes with a basic pH, but sulfate-based hardness (calcium sulfate, Epsom salt) can come with a low pH.
Clean, bacteria-free water matters more for fish than the exact GH value.
Recommended GH for most freshwater tanks: 4–8 dGH (70–140 ppm).
Soft-water fish such as discus need GH lowered to 3 dGH (50 ppm) or below; livebearers, goldfish and African cichlids prefer higher GH.
Target GH for Neocaridina shrimp is 4 to 10 dGH; for Caridina shrimp 4 to 6 dGH.
Low GH in fish can show as poor appetite, slow growth, lethargy or faded colours.
Low GH can cause molting problems in shrimp and thin, flaking or pitted snail shells.
Low GH can cause calcium and other mineral deficiencies in plants; magnesium deficiency shows as lighter leaves with dark veins.
Too low GH can leave shrimp with a soft shell they struggle to break out of; too high GH makes the shell too tough so the shrimp gets stuck while molting.
Signs of too high GH in shrimp tanks include failed molts and mineral buildup near the waterline, but other causes give these too, so test GH.
GH that is too high makes gas exchange through fish gills harder and makes shrimp shells thick and hard to molt.
GH above about 11 dGH can encourage algae outbreaks, especially hair algae.
GH rises from water changes with harder water, topping off with tap or tank water instead of RO/distilled water, and hardscape rocks containing calcium.
GH falls from water changes with softer water and from Seachem CupriSorb in the filter.
Limestone rocks used in aquascapes such as đá kẹp kem, đá da voi and đá tai mèo are a main source of GH in tanks.
API GH test: rinse the tube with tank water, fill to 5 mL, add GH reagent one drop at a time, shaking after each, until the colour turns from orange to green.
API GH test: the number of drops is the dGH; multiply the drops by 17.9 to get mg/L.
Test at the same time of day with a fresh sample, and store the kit dry, out of direct sunlight and heat.
To raise GH, crushed coral is the first choice: about 1 lb per 10 gallons mixed into the substrate or in a media bag, replaced every 6–12 months; it dissolves faster at lower pH.
Wonder Shells or Seachem Equilibrium can be used instead of crushed coral to raise GH.
Cuttlebone can be added to raise GH; crushed coral raises KH and pH as well.
If tap water is already hard, extra water changes are enough to raise GH.
Limestone raises both GH and KH; to raise GH alone, use calcium and magnesium sources without carbonates.
Adding minerals ('châm khoáng') raises GH, and dissolving đá kẹp kem raises GH and pH.
To lower GH, mix in softer water such as rainwater or reverse osmosis water, or use a cation exchanger.
Seachem Discus Buffer and Acid Regulator are said to lower hardness by precipitating calcium and magnesium.
Lowering GH with RO: at GH 10 and KH 5, replacing 10% of the water with RO gives about GH 9 and KH 4.5; this also dilutes KH, pH and TDS.
Lower GH gradually by mixing in RODI water and keeping water changes small, letting the tank soften over time.
Top off evaporation with RO or distilled water, not tap water, to stop hardness creeping up.
Shrimp prefer stability above almost everything else: change one method at a time, make changes slowly (e.g. 10% water changes), and act only on symptoms or a big deviation.
Test GH regularly instead of assuming it is fine.
A normal GH reading can hide a calcium–magnesium imbalance: high magnesium with too little calcium; test calcium separately with a freshwater calcium kit.
Magnesium above about 10 mg/l can hinder calcium uptake.
Using GH, KH and other hardness terms interchangeably is a common error.
KH is usually lower than GH but can be higher when other carbonates such as sodium hydrogen carbonate are present, so GH should not be assumed equal to KH.
Using fully demineralised RO water without remineralising or mixing it leaves too few important minerals.
Letting GH drop below what animals and plants need can lead to poor growth or death.
Making large or fast GH changes is a mistake in shrimp tanks.
aquariumscience.org says the belief that Lake Malawi water is very hard is wrong.
aquariumscience.org says the research does not support the idea that high GH is needed for healthy fish or fry.
aquariumscience.org says a published claim that guppy fry do best at 900 ppm GH is impossible with calcium carbonate (maximum about 350 ppm) and likely off by a factor of ten.
aquariumscience.org says 150 ppm water is not 'soft' water, though it is often called that.
Vietnam's national domestic water standard QCVN 01-1:2018/BYT allows hardness up to 300 mg/L as CaCO3 ('Độ cứng, tính theo CaCO3').
Vietnamese tap water usually has a pH of about 7.5-8.
Vietnamese shops suggest adding GH+ or calcium–magnesium mineral supplements when GH is below 4 dGH.
